subject: math
title: Matrices and Determinants
syllabus: Matrices, algebra of matrices, types of matrices, determinants and matrices of order two and three, evaluation of determinants, area of triangles using determinants, adjoint and inverse of a square matrix, test of consistency and solution of simultaneous linear equations in two or three variables using matrices.

body: A matrix is a table of numbers; AB is defined when columns of A = rows of B, and usually AB ≠ BA.
Transpose: (AB)^{T} = B^{T}A^{T}. Symmetric: A^{T} = A; skew-symmetric: A^{T} = −A (diagonal zero).
trace(A) = sum of the diagonal. trace(A^{T}A) = sum of the squares of ALL entries.
Cayley–Hamilton (2 × 2): A^{2} − (trace A)A + (det A)I = 0. Multiply by A^{−1} to get A^{−1} in terms of A and I.
A is singular when |A| = 0. A^{−1} = \f{adj A}{|A|} exists only when |A| ≠ 0.

For a matrix of order n:
|kA| = k^{n}|A|, |adj A| = |A|^{n−1}, |A^{−1}| = \f{1}{|A|}, |AB| = |A||B|, |A^{T}| = |A|
Also adj(kA) = k^{n−1}adj A and adj(adj A) = |A|^{n−2}A.
Long chains like |3 adj(2A)|: work from the INSIDE out, one rule at a time.

For AX = B with D = |A|:
D ≠ 0 → unique solution (Cramer: x = \f{D_{x}}{D}, …)
D = 0 and some D_{x}, D_{y}, D_{z} ≠ 0 → no solution.
D = 0 and all D_{x} = D_{y} = D_{z} = 0 → usually infinitely many solutions (check consistency).
Fast trick for "infinitely many": the third equation must be p × (eq 1) + q × (eq 2). Find p, q from two known coefficients, then read off λ and μ.
A homogeneous system (B = 0) always has x = y = z = 0; it has a non-trivial solution exactly when D = 0.

traps: D = 0 alone does not mean infinitely many solutions — check consistency.
"Non-trivial solution" questions are about D = 0 only.

steps.note: Unique, none or infinitely many solutions

Let A and B be two square matrices of order 3 such that |A| = 3 and |B| = 2. Then |A^{T}A(adj(2A))^{−1}(adj(4B))(adj(AB))^{−1}AA^{T}| is equal to :

sol: |(2A)^{−1}| = \f{1}{24}; each adj squares the determinant, each scalar k multiplies it by k^{3}.

pyq.q: Let A be a square matrix of order 3 such that det(A) = −2 and det(3adj(−6adj(3A))) = 2^{m+n}·3^{mn}, m > n. Then 4m + 2n is equal to ______.
Let |A| = 6, where A is a 3 × 3 matrix. If |adj(3adj(A^{2}·adj(2A)))| = 2^{m}·3^{n}, m, n ∈ N, then m + n is equal to ______.

Let A = [[cos θ, 0, −sin θ], [0, 1, 0], [sin θ, 0, cos θ]]. If for some θ ∈ (0, π), A^{2} = A^{T}, then the sum of the diagonal elements of the matrix (A + I)^{3} + (A − I)^{3} − 6A is equal to ______.
Let A be a 2 × 2 symmetric matrix such that A[1, 1]^{T} = [3, 7]^{T} and the determinant of A be 1. If A^{−1} = αA + βI, where I is an identity matrix of order 2 × 2, then α + β equals ______.
sol: Cayley–Hamilton: A^{2} − 6A + I = 0 → A^{−1} = 6I − A → α = −1, β = 6.

pyq.q: The number of singular matrices of order 2, whose elements are from the set {2, 3, 6, 9}, is ______.
sol: Singular ⇔ ad = bc. List the 16 ordered products ad and how often each occurs: 4 (1), 6 (2), 9 (1), 12 (2), 18 (4), 27 (2), 36 (1), 54 (2), 81 (1).
For each product value, (a, d) and (b, c) can each be any of its pairs → Σ (count)^{2} = 1 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 16 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 36.

pyq.q: Let A = [a_{ij}] be a square matrix of order 2 with entries either 0 or 1. Let E be the event that A is an invertible matrix. Then the probability P(E) is :
sol: 16 matrices in all. det = ad − bc ≠ 0 needs exactly one of ad, bc to be 1.
ad = 1, bc = 0: 3 ways; ad = 0, bc = 1: 3 ways → 6.

pyq.q: Let A = [a_{ij}] be a 2 × 2 matrix such that a_{ij} ∈ {0, 1} for all i and j. Let the random variable X denote the possible values of the determinant of the matrix A. Then, the variance of X is :
The number of 3 × 2 matrices A, which can be formed using the elements of the set {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2} such that the sum of all the diagonal elements of A^{T}A is 5, is ______.
sol: trace(A^{T}A) = sum of squares of all 6 entries = 5.
Either one ±2 and one ±1 (6 × 5 × 4 = 120 ways) or five ±1 and one 0 (6 × 2^{5} = 192 ways).

The values of m, n, for which the system of equations x + y + z = 4, 2x + 5y + 5z = 17, x + 2y + mz = n has infinitely many solutions, satisfy the equation :
sol: First two equations give x = 1, y + z = 3; third: 1 + 2(y + z) = n → n = 7.

pyq.q: If the system of equations 11x + y + λz = −5, 2x + 3y + 5z = 3, 8x − 19y − 39z = μ has infinitely many solutions, then λ^{4} − μ is equal to :
sol: Row 3 = 2 × row 1 − 7 × row 2 on the left, so μ = 2(−5) − 7(3) = −31.

pyq.q: If the system of equations 2x + 7y + λz = 3, 3x + 2y + 5z = 4, x + μy + 32z = −1 has infinitely many solutions, then (λ − μ) is equal to ______.
sol: Infinitely many solutions → equation 3 = p × (eq 1) + q × (eq 2). Use the x-coefficients and the right sides: 2p + 3q = 1, 3p + 4q = −1 → q = 5, p = −7.

Let the system of equations x + 5y − z = 1, 4x + 3y − 3z = 7, 24x + y + λz = μ, λ, μ ∈ R, have infinitely many solutions. Then the number of the solutions of this system, if x, y, z are integers and satisfy 7 ≤ x + y + z ≤ 77, is :
sol: With infinitely many solutions, every solution of the first two equations works (λ = −17, μ = 45).
From eq 1: x = 1 − 5y + z. Put in eq 2: −17y + z = 3 → z = 17y + 3, x = 12y + 4 — integers for every integer y.

pyq.q: If the system of equations x + 4y − z = λ, 7x + 9y + μz = −3, 5x + y + 2z = −1 has infinitely many solutions, then (2μ + 3λ) is equal to :
sol: Eq 2 must be p × (eq 1) + q × (eq 3): x: p + 5q = 7, y: 4p + q = 9 → p = 2, q = 1.

sol: No solution needs D = 0: D = 19 − α → α = 19.
Then D_{x} ≠ 0, so the system is inconsistent.

pyq.q: The system of equations x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 5z = 9, x + 5y + λz = μ, has no solution if
sol: D = λ − 17 → singular only for λ = 17.
With λ = 17, row 3 = 4 × row 2 − 3 × row 1 on the left, so consistency needs μ = 36 − 18 = 18.

pyq.q: If the system of equations 2x − y + z = 4, 5x + λy + 3z = 12, 100x − 47y + μz = 212 has infinitely many solutions, then μ − 2λ is equal to
sol: Eq 3 = p × (eq 1) + q × (eq 2) on x and the right side: 2p + 5q = 100, 4p + 12q = 212 → q = 6, p = 35.

pyq.q: If the system of equations x + 2y − 3z = 2, 2x + λy + 5z = 5, 14x + 3y + μz = 33 has infinitely many solutions, then λ + μ is equal to :
sol: Row 3 = p·row 1 + q·row 2 with RHS: 2p + 5q = 33 and p + 2q = 14 → q = 5, p = 4.

pyq.q: If the system of equations: x + y + z = 5, x + 2y + 3z = 9, x + 3y + λz = μ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of λ + μ is:
sol: Row 3 = 2 × row 2 − row 1 on x, y → z: 6 − 1 = 5 = λ; RHS: 18 − 5 = 13 = μ.

pyq.q: The system of linear equations x + y + z = 6, 2x + 5y + az = 36, x + 2y + 3z = b has
sol: D = 8 − a → a = 8 makes the system singular.
Row 3 = \f{1}{3}(row 1 + row 2) on the left → b = \f{6 + 36}{3} = 14 for consistency.
a = 8, b = 14 → infinitely many solutions (b = 16 → none).
o: unique solution for a = 8 and b = 16
infinitely many solutions for a = 8 and b = 14
infinitely many solutions for a = 8 and b = 16
unique solution for a = 8 and b = 14

pyq.q: If the system of linear equations: x + y + z = 6, x + 2y + 5z = 10, 2x + 3y + λz = μ has infinitely many solutions, then the value of λ + μ equals:
sol: Row 3 = row 1 + row 2 on x, y → λ = 1 + 5 = 6 and μ = 6 + 10 = 16.
